Binaries for all six shipped architectures are attached to the GitHub release, each checksummed and signed. And once it's installed, that one binary can cross-compile your programs to any of the eleven — see Cross-compilation.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.11: The Compiler Catches More of Your Mistakes
docs.text: The whole promise of Stenopos is that the compiler catches your mistakes before your users do. beta.11 makes it catch a few more — the shipped compiler now rejects the same bad programs the reference compiler always has, and explains them the same way.

docs.title: A little background
docs.text:
Stenopos is written in Stenopos. There are really two compilers: the original one (written in Rust, the "reference"), and the self-hosted one (written in Stenopos, which is what you download). For a long time the self-hosted compiler could build everything the reference could — but it was quietly a bit more lenient: a handful of clearly-wrong programs slipped through it that the reference would have stopped.

For a language whose pitch is "the compiler is on your side," being less strict than the reference is exactly the wrong direction. beta.11 closes the gap.

docs.title: What it now catches
docs.text:
Four kinds of mistake that used to slip through the shipped compiler now stop it:

Returning the wrong type. A function that promises to return an int32 but hands back a true:

func f() -> int32 {
    return true      // error: return type mismatch
}

A match that forgets a case. If you match on an enum, you have to handle every variant (or add a case _). Miss one, and the compiler says so — instead of silently letting a value fall through with nowhere to go:

match (color) {
    case Color.Red: paint_red()
    // error: match is not exhaustive — Green and Blue aren't handled
}

A contract that isn't a yes/no question. @requires and @ensures are boolean conditions; anything else is now rejected:

@requires(n)         // error: a `@requires` contract must be a `bool` expression
func f(int32 n) -> int32 { return n }

A struct built with a field missing. Leave one out and the compiler names it, instead of a confusing punctuation error:

Point p = Point { x: 1 }   // error: struct literal for `Point` is missing field `y`

docs.title: Clearer wording, too
docs.text: A few messages were reworded to match the reference exactly — an unknown name now reads undefined variable `x`, and a type that needs a cast[T]() says "no implicit conversions." Small, but it means every tool and tutorial describes the same error the same way.

docs.title: The proof
docs.text: There's a public suite of example programs — real code and deliberately-broken code — that every release is checked against. As of beta.11 the shipped, self-hosted compiler passes all 55 of them, the broken ones included. What the reference rejects, the compiler you download now rejects too.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

Nothing in your working code needs to change — if your programs were correct, they still compile. beta.11 only turns a few incorrect programs from "compiles anyway" into "here's what's wrong."

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.12: Safer, and Faster
docs.text: Two things a systems language owes you: it shouldn't let you write a memory bug, and it shouldn't make you pay for that safety in speed. beta.12 pushes on both — the compiler catches two more kinds of mistake before your program ever runs, and the code it produces got noticeably faster.

docs.title: Using something before it exists
docs.text:
You can declare a variable and fill it in later. But what if one path forgets to?

func pick() -> int32 {
    int32 x
    if (lucky()) {
        x = 10
    }
    return x        // error: `x` may be used before it is assigned
}

Before, a program like this could read whatever happened to be sitting in memory — the classic source of "works on my machine, crashes on yours," and worse. Now the compiler traces every path through your function, and if even one of them reaches a read without a write first, it stops you and points at the spot. If you meant for it to start at zero, say so (int32 x = 0) — but now that's your choice, not an accident.

(Anything that lives on the heap and is declared without a value is zeroed, so an early read can never hand back a dangling pointer. Safe by construction.)

docs.title: Dividing by zero the compiler can already see
docs.text:
If the compiler can tell the divisor is zero, there's no reason to wait until the program runs to find out:

int32 bad  = 10 / 0        // error: division by zero
int32 also = x % (3 - 3)   // error: division by zero

Divisors it can't know until runtime still trap safely — this just moves the obvious cases to compile time, where a mistake is cheap to fix.

docs.title: Faster, without giving up the checks
docs.text:
Stenopos checks things C doesn't: every array index is in bounds, every +, -, and * is watched for overflow. Those checks are why a whole category of exploits simply can't happen here. The catch has always been that checks cost time.

beta.12 gets most of that time back. For a lot of everyday code, the compiler now proves that a check can never fire — and when it can prove it, it removes the check. A loop that sums an array, a counter that can't overflow, an index that's plainly in range: the safety is still guaranteed, but the machine code comes out the same as the unchecked C you'd have written by hand. Several of our benchmarks that used to run meaningfully slower than C now match it exactly.

You don't switch any of this on. Build your program, and it's just faster.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

As always, correct programs keep working unchanged. beta.12 only turns a few incorrect ones from "compiles, then misbehaves" into "here's the line" — and makes the correct ones run faster on the way out.

docs.title: Stenopos compiles itself, and the Rust is gone
docs.text: v1.0.0-rc.1 is out, and it crosses a line the whole project was pointed at from the start: Stenopos is now written in Stenopos, and nothing else. The compiler that turns your .sten files into programs was itself built by a compiler written in the same language — no Rust anywhere.

docs.title: How a language gets off the ground
docs.text:
Every new language faces the same chicken-and-egg problem. To compile Stenopos, you need a Stenopos compiler. But to write the compiler in Stenopos, you'd need a Stenopos compiler to compile it. Something has to come first.

So Stenopos started with a seed: a compiler for Stenopos, written in Rust. It wasn't the goal — it was scaffolding. Its only job was to compile the real compiler, the one written in Stenopos, until that one could stand on its own.

For the last stretch of betas, that's exactly what happened. The Stenopos-written compiler learned to build everything the Rust seed could, then to reject the same mistakes the same way, and lately to run some things faster than the seed did. It quietly became the compiler you actually download.

docs.title: What just changed
docs.text:
With rc.1, the scaffolding comes down. The Rust seed — about 66,000 lines — is deleted. What's left builds itself:

  • The compiler compiles its own source into a new compiler.
  • That new compiler compiles the source again.
  • The two outputs come out byte-for-byte identical — a fixed point. That's the proof it's stable: a compiler that reproduces itself exactly.

Think of it like a printing press that can print the complete plans for building another press just like it — and the copy it prints is indistinguishable from the original. Once you have one working press, you never need the workshop that built the first one again.

To make that reproducible for anyone, each release ships a seed of record: one trusted, prebuilt Stenopos binary. Point the build at it and it reconstructs the whole compiler from source, start to finish, with no Rust toolchain on the machine at all. We even run the build with cargo and rustc replaced by tripwires that fail if anything tries to call them — and it sails through.

docs.title: What this means for you
docs.text:
Nothing in your code has to change. The language is the same, your programs compile and run the same, and the binaries you download work the same way. This is a change in how the compiler is made, not in what it does.

What it buys the project is honesty and independence: the tool that promises to catch your mistakes is now held to its own promises. Every safety guarantee Stenopos makes — memory safety, checked arithmetic, taint tracking — the compiler's own source code lives under. It eats its own cooking.

docs.title: The road here, briefly
docs.text: The betas were the climb: null safety, the trait system, diagnostics that match to the letter, six shipped CPU architectures, checked-overflow and bounds elision that claw back the speed, and last-use move elision. Every one of those had to work in the Stenopos-written compiler before the Rust could go. rc.1 is where the ladder gets kicked away.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

A release candidate means we think this is what 1.0 looks like. If your programs were correct, they still are — now built by a compiler that speaks its own language.

docs.title: rc.2: closures, a security type system, and a smarter scheduler
docs.text:
v1.0.0-rc.2 is the biggest feature release since the language started compiling itself. Three things landed at once — lambdas, a security type system you can actually feel at compile time, and a concurrency scheduler that stops treating every background task as a brand-new operating-system thread.

Everything here was written in Stenopos, compiled by Stenopos, and checked the same way every release is: the compiler builds itself twice and the two results come out byte-for-byte identical.

docs.title: Lambdas: functions you can hand around
docs.text:
Until now, a function was a thing you named and called. You couldn't pick one up and pass it somewhere. Now you can:

List[int32] xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
List[int32] doubled = xs.map(|x| -> int32 x * 2)   // 2 4 6 8 10
List[int32] evens   = xs.filter(|x| x % 2 == 0)     // 2 4
int32 total         = xs.reduce(0, |acc, x| acc + x) // 15

A |x| ... is a lambda — a small function written right where you use it. It can also capture values from around it (by copy, so the original is never disturbed):

int32 factor = 10
fn(int32)->int32 scale = |x| -> int32 x * factor   // remembers factor = 10

map, filter, and reduce on lists come along for free. The type fn(int32)->int32 is a real type you can store in a variable, pass to a function, or return from one.

docs.title: A type system that enforces security
docs.text:
This is the part we're most excited about. Stenopos now tracks, at compile time, five different ways code can go wrong with sensitive data — and refuses to build a program that gets them wrong.

  • @sensitive wipes secrets. Mark a value @sensitive and its memory is zeroed the moment it's done being used, so a key or password can't linger in freed memory for a crash dump or a later read to find.

  • Capability tokens (cap[R]). A function can only touch the filesystem, the network, and so on if it is handed a token for it. You can't conjure one out of thin air — only trusted code mints them, and they're passed along explicitly. Code that was never given the token simply cannot reach the resource.

  • An effect lattice (@pure → @io → @net). Label a function with what it's allowed to do and the compiler checks it — and everything it calls — stays inside that box. A @pure function provably does nothing you can observe; an @io function provably never opens a socket.

  • Constant-time secrets (secret[T]). A secret[int32] can't be used in a way whose timing would leak it — no branching on it, no using it as an array index, no division. You get ct_select to choose between two values without a branch, and declassify to say, out loud and on the record, "I am revealing this now."

  • --obfuscate. Build with this flag and the text strings in your program are scrambled on disk, so running strings on the binary turns up nothing. They're unscrambled in memory the instant the program starts.

None of this slows down code that doesn't opt in. It's there when you reach for it.

docs.title: Hemerodromes that reuse threads
docs.text:
spawn starts a Hemerodrome — a concurrent unit of work. Before rc.2, every spawn created a fresh operating-system thread. That's fine for a handful; it's wasteful for thousands.

Now Hemerodromes run on a pool of worker threads that get reused. When you spawn work, an idle worker picks it up; the pool only grows a new thread when every worker is already busy. So short tasks stop costing a whole thread each, and a task that blocks can never starve the others — the behavior is never worse than before, and usually much better. Your code doesn't change at all; spawn, channels, and locks work exactly as they did.

Along the way we found and fixed a quiet bug: the machinery behind try/catch was shared across threads when it shouldn't have been. Each Hemerodrome now has its own, so a throw in one can never trip over another's. The thread-safety checkers agree it's clean.

docs.title: Getting it
docs.text:
Same as always — grab the compiler, point it at a .sten file, and run it. The full list of changes is in the changelog.

Next up: inline assembly, which unlocks the last piece of the scheduler and a path to running Stenopos with no C runtime underneath at all.

docs.title: rc.3: a language server, data that moves between threads, and raw assembly
docs.text:
v1.0.0-rc.3 makes Stenopos feel like a language you live in, not just one you compile with. Your editor now understands it, concurrent tasks can hand real data back and forth without copying or races, and — for the rare moments you need it — you can drop all the way down to raw machine instructions.

As always, everything here was written in Stenopos, compiled by Stenopos, and checked the same way: the compiler builds itself twice and the two results come out byte-for-byte identical.

docs.title: Your editor now understands Stenopos
docs.text:
Stenopos ships a language server. Point any editor that speaks LSP — VS Code, Neovim, and most others — at stenopos lsp, and you get:

  • Live error checking. As you type, mistakes get a red underline with the real compiler's message — the exact same check that runs at build time, not a rough imitation. Fix the problem and the underline disappears.
  • Hover a name to see what it is.
  • Jump to definition of a function, struct, or enum.
  • Completion for keywords, built-ins, and the names in your file.

It's one command — the language server is built into the stenopos binary, nothing extra to install. Setup for Neovim and VS Code is in the docs.

docs.title: Passing real data between Hemerodromes
docs.text:
A Hemerodrome is a concurrent unit of work you start with spawn. Until now, the mailbox between Hemerodromes — a channel — could only carry simple numbers. Now it carries real things: text, structs, lists, and maps.

chan[str] ch = chan()
spawn producer(ch)
str msg = ch.recv()        // a whole string arrives, safely

The trick is a simple rule: sending gives the value away. When you send something down a channel, the sender no longer owns it — the receiver does. There is never a moment where two Hemerodromes both hold the same piece of memory, so there's no race and nothing gets freed twice. The compiler enforces this for you; if you want to keep a copy, you say so with .clone(). And because sending is a handover, not a copy, it costs the same whether you send three characters or three megabytes.

Locks learned the same lesson. A mutex[Point] can guard a real struct, and you can change it in place while you hold the lock — no copying it out and back:

with (p = m.borrow()) {
    p.x = p.x + 1          // changed right where it lives, under the lock
}

That borrow is fenced in: the compiler won't let the pointer escape the locked section, so you can't accidentally keep using it after the lock is released. There's a read-only version, read_borrow(), for when many readers just want to look.

docs.title: Inline assembly
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to say exactly what the machine does. asm { } lets you write raw instructions, with the GCC-style operand syntax for feeding values in and getting them out:

unsafe {
    asm {
        "addl %1, %0"
        : "=r"(sum)
        : "r"(a), "r"(b)
    }
}

It's gated behind unsafe, because it is. This is the last piece the green-thread scheduler needed for its hand-written context switch — and it opens the path to running Stenopos with no C runtime underneath at all.

docs.title: Smaller and quicker, too
docs.text: Calls between functions in the same program now go directly to their target instead of through an indirection table, the way a C compiler does it — a little less overhead and a little smaller on disk, for free.

docs.title: Getting it
docs.text:
Same as always — grab the compiler, point it at a .sten file, and run it. The full list of changes is in the changelog.

Next up: making the editor smarts deeper — hover and go-to-definition that follow the compiler's full understanding of your code, across files — and the final polish on the road to 1.0.

docs.title: If / else
docs.text:
Parentheses around the condition are required:

if (x > 0) {
    println("positive")
} else if (x < 0) {
    println("negative")
} else {
    println("zero")
}

docs.title: Ternary
docs.text: int32 abs_x = if (x >= 0) x else -x

docs.title: For loops
docs.text:
// inclusive range (0 through 9)
for (i in 0..9) {
    println("{i}")
}

// exclusive range (0 through 9, not 10)
for (i in 0..<10) {
    println("{i}")
}

docs.title: While
docs.text:
while (counter < 100) {
    counter = counter + 1
}

docs.title: Do-while
docs.text:
do {
    counter = counter + 1
} while (counter < 100)

docs.title: Repeat
docs.text:
repeat (5) {
    println("hello")
}

docs.title: Match
docs.text:
A case uses the colon form: the statements after the : run until the next case or the closing }. Patterns can be literals, inclusive (..) or exclusive (..<) ranges, or _ for the catch-all.

match (status) {
    case 200: println("OK")
    case 404: println("Not found")
    case 500..599: println("Server error")
    case _: println("Unknown: {status}")
}

A case can run several statements — they all belong to the case until the next case:

match (status) {
    case 200:
        log("serving")
        println("OK")
    case _:
        println("Unknown: {status}")
}

Enum variants match by their qualified name, and payload fields bind as names:

match (shape) {
    case Shape.Circle(r): return 3.14159 * r * r
    case Shape.Rect(w, h): return w * h
    case Shape.Empty: return 0.0
}

docs.title: Break and continue
docs.text:
for (i in 0..<100) {
    if (i == 50) {
        break
    }
    if (i % 2 == 0) {
        continue
    }
    println("{i}")
}

docs.title: Try / catch / finally
docs.text:
try {
    str content = read_file("data.txt")
    process(content)
} catch (IOError e) {
    println("File error: {e.message}")
} catch (Error e) {
    println("Unexpected error: {e.message}")
} finally {
    cleanup()
}

The finally block always runs, whether or not an error occurred.

docs.title: With (resource cleanup)
docs.text:
The with block closes resources automatically, even if an error occurs:

with (File f = open("log.txt")) {
    f.write("entry\n")
}
// f is closed here

docs.title: Defer
docs.text:
defer schedules an expression to run when its enclosing block exits — by any path: falling off the end, an early return, a break/continue, or a throw. Deferred expressions run last-in-first-out, and before the block's locals are freed, so cleanup can still use them.

func process() -> void {
    File f = open("data.txt")
    defer f.close()          // runs no matter how process() exits

    str line = f.read_line()
    // ... f.close() runs here automatically ...
}

defer is block-scoped: a defer inside a loop body fires at the end of each iteration, not all at once when the function returns.

for (i in 0..2) {
    defer println("close {i}")
    println("open {i}")
}
// open 0 / close 0 / open 1 / close 1 / open 2 / close 2

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
@requires and @ensures attach a precondition and a postcondition to a function. Both are boolean expressions checked at run time; @ensures also sees the returned value as result. A violated contract reports which one failed and stops the program — a broken assumption halts at the boundary that stated it, instead of corrupting whatever comes next.

@requires(n >= 0)
@ensures(result >= 1)
func factorial(int32 n) -> int32 {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
}

Several @requires may be stacked; each is checked on entry.

docs.title: Nested error handling
docs.text:
func load_and_process(str path) -> void {
    try {
        str data = read_file(path)
        try {
            parse(data)
        } catch (ParseError e) {
            println("Bad format: {e.message}")
        }
    } catch (IOError e) {
        println("Cannot read {path}: {e.message}")
    }
}

docs.text:
Evaluated at compile time when all arguments are constants:

const func factorial(int32 n) -> int32 {

docs.title: Memory Safety
docs.text: Stenopos uses NOVA (No Overhead Value Allocation) to manage heap memory automatically — without a garbage collector and without manual free calls.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When a value goes out of scope, the compiler inserts a free call automatically. There is no runtime overhead beyond the allocation itself.

func process() -> void {
    str data = read_file("input.txt")   // heap allocation
    println("{data}")
    // data is freed here automatically — end of scope
}

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Each value has one owner. When you assign a value to a new variable, ownership transfers (a move):

str a = "hello"
str b = a       // 'a' is moved into 'b'
// println(a)    // compile error — 'a' was moved
println(b)       // ok

docs.title: Borrow checker
docs.text:
The borrow checker prevents use-after-move at compile time, with no runtime checks needed.

str message = "hello"
str other = message      // move
println(message)          // error: value was moved

docs.title: Raw pointers
docs.text:
For C interoperability, raw pointers are available — but only in unsafe blocks:

extern "C" func malloc(uint64 size) -> ptr[void]

unsafe {
    ptr[int32] p = cast[ptr[int32]](malloc(4))
    *p = 42
    int32 val = *p
}

docs.title: No null pointer dereferences
docs.text:
Nullable pointers use ptr[T]? syntax and must be checked before use:

ptr[int32]? maybe = find_value()
if (maybe != null) {
    unsafe {
        int32 val = *maybe
    }
}

docs.text: module math.vector

docs.title: Visibility: pub vs. private
docs.text:
Declarations are private to their module by default. A function, struct, enum, trait, or type alias is only visible to code in the same module unless you mark it pub. Reaching for a private name from another module is a compile error:

module math.internal

pub func cube(int32 n) -> int32 {   // public API — callable anywhere
    return n * square(n)
}

func square(int32 n) -> int32 {     // private — only this module may use it
    return n * n
}

module app.main

import math.internal.{cube}

func main() -> void {
    println("{cube(3)}")            // ok — cube is pub
    // println("{square(3)}")       // compile error: square is private to math.internal
}

This keeps a module's surface area deliberate: callers depend only on what you chose to expose, and you can refactor everything else freely.

docs.title: Language Guide Overview
docs.text: Stenopos is a statically typed systems language with C-style brace syntax and no semicolons. This guide walks through the core language features.

docs.title: Design goals
docs.text:
• Readable — curly-brace blocks, no semicolons
  • Safe by default — memory safety, taint tracking, effect types built into the type system
  • C-compatible — call any C library with zero overhead
  • Single binary — one tool for build, run, test, format, lint

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Variables and Types
  • Functions
  • Control Flow
  • Structs and Classes
  • Memory Safety
  • Error Handling
  • Modules

docs.title: Structs
docs.text:
Plain data containers that live on the stack:

struct Point {
    float64 x
    float64 y
}

Point p = Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }
println("{p.x}, {p.y}")

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Classes support inheritance and live on the heap (managed by NOVA):

class Animal {
    pub str name

    virtual func speak() -> void {
        println("...")
    }
}

class Dog : Animal {
    override func speak() -> void {
        println("Woof! I'm {this.name}")
    }
}

Use parent to call the parent class method:

class Puppy : Dog {
    override func speak() -> void {
        parent.speak()
        println("*wags tail*")
    }
}

docs.title: Abstract classes
docs.text:
class Shape {
    abstract func area() -> float64

    virtual func describe() -> str {
        return "a shape"
    }
}

class Circle : Shape {
    pub float64 radius

    override func area() -> float64 {
        return 3.14159 * this.radius * this.radius
    }
}

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text:
Fields and methods are private by default. Use pub or protected:

class BankAccount {
    float64 balance                 // private (default)

    pub func deposit(float64 amount) -> void {
        balance += amount
    }

    pub func get_balance() -> float64 {
        return balance
    }

    protected func audit_log() -> void {
        // only this class and subclasses
    }
}

docs.title: Traits
docs.text:
trait Printable {
    func print() -> void
}

impl Printable for Point {
    func print() -> void {
        println("({this.x}, {this.y})")
    }
}

docs.title: Adding traits to existing types
docs.text:
impl Printable for Circle {
    func print() -> void {
        println("Circle r={this.radius}")
    }
}

docs.title: Statements & Line Breaks
docs.text:
Stenopos uses newline as the statement terminator — like Go, and unlike C. There are no semicolons. Write one statement per line:

int32 x = 42
int32 y = x + 1
println("{y}")

Blank lines are ignored, so use them freely to group code. Indentation is not significant (blocks are delimited by braces), but 4-space indentation is the convention.

docs.title: Breaking a long line
docs.text: A newline ends a statement only when the line so far could be a complete statement. In the two situations below the newline is treated as a space and the statement continues — the same rule Go uses. There is no line-continuation character (a \ is not special here).

docs.title: 1. After an operator that needs a right-hand side
docs.text:
A line that ends on an operator which cannot finish a statement — a binary, comparison, logical, bitwise, or assignment operator, ??, a trailing ., or -> — continues onto the next line:

int32 total = first_value +
              second_value +
              third_value

if (ready &&
    count > 0) {
    // ...
}

Method-call chains break the same way, on a trailing .:

str result = name.trim().
    to_upper()

(The . must end the upper line. A line that ends on a complete value — e.g. name.trim() — terminates, so a .method() cannot start the next line.)

docs.title: 2. Inside brackets ( … ) and [ … ]
docs.text:
Newlines between a matching (/) or [/] are ignored, so call arguments, function parameters, array/list literals, and parenthesized expressions may span lines:

int32 s = add(
    add(1, 2),
    add(3, 4))

func distance(float64 x,
              float64 y) -> float64 {
    return x * x + y * y
}

int32[3] triple = [10,
                   20,
                   30]

No trailing comma

Close the list right after the last element (3) above, not 3,)). A trailing comma before the closing bracket is a syntax error.

docs.title: String interpolation
docs.text:
Inside an interpolated string, "{ ... }" holds an expression that is evaluated and formatted in place. The whole string literal stays on a single source line:

str name = "Stenopos"
println("Hello, {name}! 1 + 1 = {1 + 1}")

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: You want to… Do this End a statement Start a new line (no ;) Continue a long expression End the line on an operator (+, &&, =, a trailing ., …) — it carries to the next line Spread call args / parameters / a list literal Break after a comma inside (…) or […] — no trailing comma Group code visually Use blank lines (ignored)

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text:
Variables are declared with the type before the name — C style, not Rust style.

int32 x = 42
int64 big = 1_000_000
float64 pi = 3.14159
str greeting = "hello"
bool flag = true

docs.title: Mutable by default
docs.text:
All variables are mutable. Use const to make something immutable:

const int32 MAX = 100
int32 counter = 0
counter = counter + 1   // ok
// MAX = 200            // compile error

docs.title: Numeric types
docs.text:
Type Size Range int32 32-bit signed -2^31 to 2^31-1 int64 64-bit signed -2^63 to 2^63-1 uint32 32-bit unsigned 0 to 2^32-1 uint64 64-bit unsigned 0 to 2^64-1 float32 32-bit float IEEE 754 float64 64-bit float IEEE 754

No implicit numeric conversions. Use cast[T]() to convert explicitly:

int32 x = 42
int64 y = cast[int64](x)

docs.title: Integer overflow is checked
docs.text:
Arithmetic that overflows its type is a bug — and a frequent source of security holes, where a wrapped size calculation leads to an undersized buffer. Stenopos does not let it happen silently. Every +, -, and * on an integer (signed or unsigned) is checked; if the result does not fit the type, the program stops with a diagnostic instead of wrapping to a wrong value:

int32 x = 2147483647    // int32 max
int32 y = x + 1         // aborts: "integer overflow: add of two int32 values"

This applies to compound assignments (+=, -=, *=) too. In-range arithmetic is unaffected, and the check is cheap — it compiles to an add plus a jump-on-overflow, not a software division.

docs.title: Opting out: wrapping_*
docs.text:
Some algorithms want modular arithmetic — hashes, checksums, PRNGs, ring-buffer indices. For those, ask for wrapping explicitly with wrapping_add, wrapping_sub, and wrapping_mul:

// FNV-1a hash — defined in terms of wrapping arithmetic, so it says so.
func fnv1a(str s) -> uint32 {
    uint32 hash = 2166136261
    int64 i = 0
    while (i < s.len()) {
        hash = wrapping_mul(hash, 16777619)
        hash = wrapping_add(hash, cast[uint32](s.byte_at(i)))
        i += 1
    }
    return hash
}

The default is safe; wrapping is opt-in and visible at the call site.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
int64 numbers[5] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
int64 first = numbers[0]

Array access is bounds-checked at compile time where possible.

docs.title: Nullable types
docs.text:
Any type T has a nullable form T? that holds either a value or null. The compiler will not let you use a T? as a T until you have ruled out null.

int32? maybe = null
str? name = "Stenopos"

Compare against null with == / !=. After a check, the value is narrowed to the non-nullable type for the rest of that scope:

func classify(int32? n) -> str {
    if (n == null) {
        return "none"
    }
    // n is narrowed to plain int32 here
    return "value: {n}"
}

Three operators work on nullables:

int32? missing = null
int32 x = missing ?? 0          // ?? — fallback when the left side is null
int32? forced = 7
int32 y = forced!!              // !! — assert non-null (aborts at runtime if null)
int64 len = name?.len() ?? 0    // ?. — safe access, yields a nullable

There is no null-pointer dereference: raw pointers are nullable with the same ptr[T]? syntax and must be checked before use inside unsafe.

docs.text:
type Meters = float64
type Seconds = float64

Meters distance = 100.0
Seconds time = 9.58

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Effect -o <output> Output binary path --release Build the release profile (alias for --profile release) --profile <name> Build a stenopos.toml profile (default: draft) --target <arch> Cross-compile (build only) — see Cross-compilation --verify-ir Run the structural IR verifier before codegen --verbose Print timing information --version Print version --help Print help 
stenopos run hello.sten
stenopos build -o myapp --release main.sten
stenopos build --target aarch64 -o app-arm64 main.sten   # cross-compile

Build profiles (stenopos.toml). stenopos build uses the draft profile (fast, unoptimized, symbols kept — best for debugging); stenopos build --release uses release (optimized, stripped, and anonymized + RE-hardened: no build-id, hidden symbols, dead code removed, and the stenopos/STENOPOS_ strings dropped so the binary looks like a generic C program). Set the default and customize in the manifest:

[build]
profile = "draft"        # profile used when you don't pass --profile

[profile.draft]
opt-level = "0"
strip = false

[profile.release]
opt-level = "2"
strip = true

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 {
    return a + b
}

func greet(str name) -> void {       // -> void is required
    println("Hello, {name}!")
}

func identity[T](T val) -> T {       // generics use [T], not <T>
    return val
}

Return values are must-use by default — a bare compute() that drops a non-void result is an error. Use it, assign it, discard compute() to drop it deliberately, or mark the function @ignore_discard.

docs.text: Group Operators Arithmetic + - * / % (overflow traps, never wraps) Comparison == != < <= > >= Logical && \|\| ! (no and/or/not) Bitwise & \| ^ ~ << >> Assignment = += -= *= /= %= &= \|= ^= <<= >>= Nullable ?. (safe access) · ?? (default) · !! docs.title: Control flow
docs.text:
if (x > 0) {
    // ...
} else if (x == 0) {
    // ...
} else {
    // ...
}

for (i in 0..10) { }        // inclusive range
for (i in 0..<10) { }       // exclusive range
for (item in list) { }
for (i, item in list) { }

while (cond) { }

match (color) {
    case Color.Red: handle_red()
    case Color.Blue: handle_blue()
    case _: handle_other()
}

One for loop covers all iteration — no foreach. Parentheses and braces are required. Newline terminates a statement (no semicolons).

docs.title: Line breaks
docs.text:
// Newline ends a statement — one per line, no semicolons.
int32 x = 42

// A line ending on an operator (that needs a right side) continues — Go's rule:
int32 y = 1 +
          2

// ...and newlines inside ( ) / [ ] are ignored (no trailing comma):
int32 t = add(a,
              b)

Continuation happens after a dangling operator (+, &&, =, a trailing ., ->, …) or inside brackets. There is no \ continuation. See Statements & Line Breaks.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
// List[T]
List[int32] xs = list_new()
xs.push(10)
int32 v = xs.get(0)         // bounds-checked
int32 first = xs.first()
int32 last = xs.last()
int32 top = xs.pop()        // remove + return last
xs.sort()                   // ascending; numeric + str elements
xs.reverse()
bool has = xs.contains(10)
int64 at = xs.index_of(10)  // first match, or -1
bool empty = xs.is_empty()
int64 n = xs.len()
xs.clear()                  // empty it, keep capacity

// HashMap[str, V]
HashMap[str, int32] ages = map_new()
ages.insert("ada", 36)
int32 a = ages.get("ada")
bool known = ages.contains("ada")

Indexing is bounds-checked and aborts on out-of-range — there is no negative indexing; use first() / last() for the ends.

docs.title: Structs, classes, enums
docs.text:
struct Point {              // private by default; pub / protected to expose
    float64 x
    float64 y
    pub func norm() -> float64 { return this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y }
}

class Dog : Animal {        // inheritance; `parent`, not `base`
    override func speak() -> void {
        parent.speak()
        println("Woof!")
    }
}

enum Color : int32 {        // backing type required
    Red = 0
    Green = 1
    Blue = 2
}
Point p = Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }

clone() is a deep copy — modifying a clone never touches the original.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
try {
    File f = open("data.txt")
} catch (IOError e) {
    log(e.message)
} finally {
    cleanup()
}

defer close(resource)       // scope cleanup (not error propagation)
throw("something failed")

try/catch/finally only — there is no ? operator.

docs.text:

int32 n = f.to_int32()              // conversion method
const_cast[T](v)                    // drop const
unsafe_cast[T](v)                   // reinterpret (unsafe)

docs.text:
str? maybe = null
if (maybe != null) {
    println(maybe.len())            // compiler narrows the type
}

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Seven keywords: spawn chan atomic mutex rwlock spinlock semaphore.

spawn worker()                      // green thread (Hemerodrome)
chan[int32] ch = chan()

counter.fetch_add(1)

mutex[int32] m = mutex(0)
with (m.guard()) {                  // scoped lock, auto-unlocks
    // ...
}

docs.title: Memory (NOVA)
docs.text:
Automatic, leak-free memory with no garbage collector. Every value has an owner; heap buffers are freed at scope exit. States used in diagnostics: Declared, Owned, Moved, Borrowed, Locked, Freed.

unsafe {
    ptr[int32] p = &x
    int32 val = *p
}

docs.title: Cross-compilation
docs.text:
Stenopos can build a binary for a different CPU than the one you are compiling on, in one command:

stenopos build --target aarch64 -o app-arm64 main.sten

That produces an ARM64 Linux executable from, say, an x86-64 laptop. No separate steps, no hand-run llc.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The compiler emits target-neutral LLVM IR — it does not bake in a CPU or a memory layout. So the same compiled program can be lowered for any supported CPU; --target just tells the backend which one, and picks the matching cross C compiler to link with.

docs.title: Supported targets
docs.text:
--target Architecture Notes x86_64 64-bit Intel/AMD the host default aarch64 (alias arm64) 64-bit ARM phones, Raspberry Pi 4/5, Apple-class ppc64le 64-bit PowerPC (little-endian) riscv64 64-bit RISC-V hard-float armv7 (alias arm) 32-bit ARM (hard-float) Raspberry Pi 2/3, many embedded boards s390x 64-bit IBM Z (big-endian) i686 (alias x86) 32-bit Intel/AMD older / smaller x86 devices mipsel 32-bit MIPS (little-endian) routers, embedded mips64el 64-bit MIPS (little-endian) powerpc (alias ppc) 32-bit PowerPC (big-endian) routers, older Macs, embedded mips 32-bit MIPS (big-endian) routers, embedded

You can pass either the short name (aarch64) or the full triple (aarch64-linux-gnu).

All eleven run correct programs — every byte order and word size (32- and 64-bit, little- and big-endian) — checked on every change, so a target on this list will not silently break.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
--target shells out to the matching cross toolchain, so it must be installed:

Target Package (Debian/Ubuntu) aarch64 gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu ppc64le gcc-powerpc64le-linux-gnu riscv64 gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu armv7 gcc-arm-linux-gnueabihf s390x gcc-s390x-linux-gnu i686 gcc-i686-linux-gnu mipsel gcc-mipsel-linux-gnu mips64el gcc-mips64el-linux-gnuabi64 powerpc gcc-powerpc-linux-gnu mips gcc-mips-linux-gnu

If the toolchain is missing, the compiler says exactly which package to install.

docs.title: Running the result
docs.text:
A cross-built binary runs on the real target device. To try it on your build machine, use an emulator:

stenopos build --target aarch64 -o app-arm64 main.sten
qemu-aarch64-static -L /usr/aarch64-linux-gnu ./app-arm64

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• --target is a build-only option — run, check, and emit-* ignore it (you cannot execute a foreign-CPU binary directly on the host).
  • Every cross build is Linux/ELF and keeps the same security hardening as a native build (PIE, full RELRO, non-executable stack, stack canaries).
  • The output is a normal ELF executable, indistinguishable in shape from a C program built with GCC for that CPU.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text: Stenopos ships as a single binary that is also your formatter, linter, doc generator, and test runner — no extra tools to install.

docs.title: stenopos fmt
docs.text:
Format source to the canonical style: 4-space indentation by brace depth, trimmed trailing whitespace, collapsed blank runs, and a single trailing newline. Comments and string contents are preserved exactly.

stenopos fmt src/main.sten          # reformat in place
stenopos fmt --check src/*.sten     # report unformatted files, exit 1 (for CI)

Formatting is idempotent — running it on already-formatted code changes nothing.

docs.title: stenopos lint
docs.text:
Report style and correctness lints over the parsed source.

stenopos lint src/*.sten

The current checks cover naming conventions (snake_case for functions and parameters, PascalCase for types and enum variants) and flag empty function bodies. Exit code is 1 if any lints are found.

docs.title: stenopos doc
docs.text:
Generate a Markdown API reference for a module's public surface — its pub functions, structs, enums, traits, and type aliases, with full signatures and the prose from their /// doc comments.

stenopos doc src/vector.sten              # print to stdout
stenopos doc src/vector.sten -o vector.md # write a file

/// Computes the area of a circle given its radius.
pub func circle_area(float64 radius) -> float64 {
    return 3.14159 * radius * radius
}

renders the signature followed by "Computes the area of a circle given its radius."

docs.title: stenopos test
docs.text:
Discover the @test functions in a file, run them, and report pass/fail.

// math_test.sten
func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 { return a + b }

@test
func test_add() -> void {
    if (add(2, 3) != 5) {
        fail("add(2, 3) should be 5")
    }
}

stenopos test math_test.sten
# running 1 test(s) from math_test.sten
# test test_add ...
# ok — 1 test(s) passed

A test signals failure by aborting (for example via fail); the runner reports a non-zero exit when any test fails.

docs.title: Debugging the compiler front end
docs.text:
When you need to see why a program parses the way it does, two subcommands expose the front end directly:

stenopos dump-tokens src/main.sten   # the lexer's token stream: line:col KIND "text"
stenopos dump-ast    src/main.sten   # the parsed AST as an indented tree

dump-ast prints each statement and its children (assignments show their target name), so you can see exactly which statements landed in which block — the fastest way to tell a lexer problem from a parser one.

docs.title: Verifying generated code
docs.text:
stenopos build --verify-ir src/main.sten   # structural IR checks before codegen

--verify-ir runs a well-formedness pass over the compiler's internal IR — every block has a terminator, every branch targets a real block, no block is unreachable — and fails the build if anything is malformed, before it can become a runaway loop or a link error. It is cheap and safe to leave on.

docs.title: stenopos explain
docs.text:
Every diagnostic is tagged with an error code — error[E0300]: .... Pass that code to stenopos explain for a long-form explanation of the whole class of problem, with guidance on how to fix it:

stenopos explain E0300

E0300 [type error]

The expected type does not match the actual type. Stenopos does not
perform implicit type conversions. Use `cast[T]()` for safe numeric
conversions or `.to_X()` methods for other conversions.

Codes are grouped by compiler phase: E01xx lexer, E02xx parser, E03xx type, E04xx memory/ownership, E05xx security. explain knows every standard code, so you can look one up straight from the error[...] tag in a build's output.

docs.title: Effect System
docs.text: The effect system lets functions declare what they do — I/O, network access, mutation, randomness. The compiler enforces those declarations.

docs.title: Effect annotations
docs.text:
@pure func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 {
    return a + b
}

@io func read_file(str path) -> str {
    // ...
}

@network @io func fetch_url(str url) -> str {
    // ...
}

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A function marked @pure cannot do I/O. You can trust it completely. This matters for:

  • Testing — pure functions are trivially testable, no mocking needed
  • Security — a math library cannot sneak in a network call
  • Parallelism — pure functions can safely run in parallel
  • Caching — pure functions can be memoized

docs.title: Inference
docs.text: Effects are inferred where possible. A function that only calls @pure functions is automatically @pure. You only need to annotate when you want to be explicit or when the inference would be wrong.

docs.title: Effect propagation
docs.text:
Calling a function with an effect requires the caller to also declare that effect:

// This would be a compile error — read_file is @io but process is not declared @io
func process(str path) -> str {
    return read_file(path)   // error: @io effect not declared
}

// Fix: declare the effect
@io func process(str path) -> str {
    return read_file(path)   // ok
}

docs.title: Security Overview
docs.text: Stenopos treats security as a type system property, not a set of runtime checks. Eight security dimensions are built into the language.

docs.title: 1. NOVA memory safety
docs.text: No dangling pointers. No use-after-free. No buffer overflows. Automatic deallocation at scope end with no GC overhead.

docs.title: 2. Taint tracking
docs.text:
User input is @tainted at the source. The compiler refuses to let tainted data reach a @sink (database query, shell command, HTML output) without going through a @sanitizer.

@tainted str user_input = request.get("name")
// db.query(user_input)         // compile error
str safe = html_escape(user_input)
response.write(safe)            // ok

docs.title: 3. Effect types
docs.text: Functions declare their side effects. A function marked @pure cannot do I/O. A function marked @io cannot make network calls unless also marked @network. This prevents supply-chain attacks where a math library sneaks in a network call.

docs.title: 4. Constant-time types
docs.text: secret[T] values cannot leak through timing side-channels. The compiler rejects branches on secret values and ensures constant-time comparison.

docs.title: 5. Contracts and refinements
docs.text: @requires and @ensures let you attach preconditions and postconditions to functions, checked at run time; inside @ensures, result names the returned value. A violated contract reports which one failed and stops the program.

docs.title: 6. Capability permissions
docs.text: cap[resource] tokens control access to system resources. Code must be explicitly granted a capability to use it — it cannot be acquired out of thin air.

docs.title: 7. Crypto safety
docs.text: @sensitive memory is wiped before deallocation and protected from compiler optimization that might eliminate the wipe.

docs.title: 8. Debug toolkit
docs.text: debug_assert, debug: blocks, and assert_main_thread for catching threading bugs in development builds.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
• NOVA memory safety — implemented
  • Taint tracking, effect types, constant-time, contracts, capabilities, crypto safety, debug toolkit — designed, not yet implemented

See Taint Tracking and Effect System for the design details.

docs.title: Taint Tracking
docs.text: Taint tracking is a compile-time data flow analysis that prevents injection attacks. It is part of the type system — not a linter, not a runtime check.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Data from external sources is marked @tainted. That taint propagates through the program. Any value derived from tainted data is also tainted. A @sink — a function that could cause harm if it receives untrusted input — refuses tainted data at compile time. A @sanitizer removes the taint by validating or escaping the data.

// Source: tainted input from the web
@tainted str name = request.get("name")

// Propagation: anything derived from 'name' is also tainted
@tainted str greeting = "Hello, " + name

// Sink: the database refuses tainted data
// db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")  // compile error

// Sanitizer: validate and escape, taint is removed
str safe_name = sql_escape(name)

// Now it can reach the sink
db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{safe_name}'")

docs.title: Declaring sources, sinks, and sanitizers
docs.text:
// A source — returns tainted data
@source func read_http_param(str key) -> @tainted str {
    // ...
}

// A sanitizer — accepts tainted, returns clean
@sanitizer func sql_escape(@tainted str input) -> str {
    // ...
}

// A sink — refuses tainted data (compiler enforces this)
@sink func db_query(str sql) -> void {
    // ...
}

docs.title: What injection attacks this prevents
docs.text:
• SQL injection
  • Command injection
  • HTML/XSS injection
  • Path traversal
  • LDAP injection
  • Any custom sink you define
